line: Did you know, Bromley's council offices were once a bishops' palace for about 700 years?
fact: The house Bromley council moved into in 1982 was the palace of the bishops of Rochester from the 1100s until 1845, when a local merchant bought it.

line: Did you know, H.G. Wells turned down the freedom of Bromley, the town he was born in?
fact: Offered the freedom of his home town, Wells said no: "Bromley has not been particularly gracious to me nor I to Bromley".

line: Did you know, H.G. Wells's father once took 4 wickets in 4 balls for Kent?
fact: Joseph Wells ran a struggling china and sports shop in Bromley. He also bowled for Kent, and in 1862 took 4 Sussex wickets in 4 balls.

line: Did you know, a Bromley coaching inn gets a mention in Jane Austen's Pride and Prejudice?
fact: Bromley was a key coaching stop on the road from London to Hastings, and Jane Austen named its Royal Bell inn in Pride and Prejudice.

line: Did you know, Bromley is named after broom, a yellow shrub that once grew all over the area?
fact: Bromley means a clearing where broom grows. In the 1800s Martin's Hill, now the war memorial garden, was one of the last places it still flowered.

place: St Peter and St Paul, Bromley
line: Did you know, Samuel Johnson came to Bromley's church in 1753 to say goodbye to his late wife?
fact: The writer's wife Tetty was buried here. He came to take leave of her, and was relieved to find his wish to marry again had cooled.
source: Wikipedia: St Peter and St Paul, Bromley

place: St Peter and St Paul, Bromley
line: Did you know, a bomb in 1941 left only the tower of Bromley's parish church standing?
fact: On the night of 16 April 1941 a bomb destroyed almost all of St Peter and St Paul but its medieval tower. The church was rebuilt around it.
source: Wikipedia: St Peter and St Paul, Bromley

line: Did you know, in 1926 Plaistow residents had a wall built to keep out working-class neighbours?
fact: Locals complained that 'vulgar' working-class people from the Downham estate were cutting through to Bromley. A wall went up and stood about 10 years.

line: Did you know, the Sundridge Park mansion was paid for by corn bought abroad when England ran short?
fact: John Nash designed it in about 1797 for Claude Scott, a corn merchant who grew rich helping the government buy foreign corn in times of scarcity.

line: Did you know, steam-powered cars were made in Shortlands in the 1910s?
fact: From 1908 to 1916 Shortlands had its own car maker, Pearson & Cox. In 1913 it built steam-powered cars and bicycles as well as small petrol cyclecars.

line: Did you know, Bromley FC's ground had its record crowd for a game against a team from Nigeria?
fact: In 1948 almost 11,000 people packed Hayes Lane for a friendly between Bromley and a Nigeria XI, the ground's record attendance.

line: Did you know, the diarist John Evelyn was robbed by highwaymen on Bromley Common?
fact: Bromley Common lay on the main road from Hastings to London and was a profitable haunt for highwaymen. In 1652 they robbed John Evelyn here.

line: Did you know, the Just William books paid for a Bromley Common house for their author and her mother?
fact: The Just William stories did so well that Richmal Crompton, once a Classics teacher, built The Glebe on Oakley Road for herself and her mother.

line: Did you know, David Bowie and Peter Frampton were taught art by Frampton's dad?
fact: In the early 1960s Bromley Technical High School's art teacher was Owen Frampton. His pupils included David Bowie and his own son Peter.

line: Did you know, the novel The Buddha of Suburbia drew on its author's years at a Bromley school?
fact: Hanif Kureishi said he was "literally the only brown person" at Bromley Technical High School. Those years fed his 1990 novel.
source: Wikipedia: Hanif Kureishi; The Buddha of Suburbia (novel)

line: Did you know, William Wilberforce decided to take on the slave trade under an oak tree at Keston?
fact: Visiting Pitt the Younger at Holwood, William Wilberforce resolved by an oak above the Keston valley to ask Parliament to end the slave trade.

line: Did you know, Pitt the Younger is thought to have flattened part of an Iron Age fort for his garden?
fact: Holwood's grounds hold an Iron Age fort called Caesar's Camp. Pitt the Younger is thought to have flattened parts of it to landscape his gardens.

line: Did you know, Keston's medieval church has no saint, just a cross called the Keston Marke?
fact: Keston's medieval church, unusually, isn't named after a saint. Its symbol instead is an ornate cross inlaid in its 17th-century altar top.

line: Did you know, Charles Darwin studied plants and animals on Keston Common for his books?
fact: Darwin's home at Down House was 2 miles away, and he often came to study the common's wildlife for his books on earthworms and meat-eating plants.

line: Did you know, 2 prime ministers, father and son, lived in a Hayes house that was knocked down in 1933?
fact: Pitt the Elder and Pitt the Younger both lived at Hayes Place, a house from the 1400s. A developer knocked it down in 1933; 2 road names recall them.

line: Did you know, an enslaved Native American man is buried in Hayes churchyard?
fact: John Panis was brought to England as a slave and died in 1763. Panis was the general word for an enslaved Native American.
source: Wikipedia: St Mary the Virgin, Hayes, Bromley

line: Did you know, local commoners stopped Hayes Common being sold off for housing in 1869?
fact: When nearby West Wickham Common was sold off for houses in the 1860s, Hayes commoners fought back. In 1869 their common won legal protection.

line: Did you know, Canadian soldiers crewed anti-aircraft guns on Hayes Common in the Second World War?
fact: During the Second World War the anti-aircraft battery on Hayes Common was manned by soldiers of the 1st Canadian Division, who lodged in local homes.

line: Did you know, David Bowie put on a free festival at a Beckenham bandstand, then wrote a song about it?
fact: In August 1969 David Bowie helped run and played a free one-day festival at this bandstand. His song Memory of a Free Festival is about it.
source: Wikipedia: Croydon Road Recreation Ground; Memory of a Free Festival

line: Did you know, a balloon carrying the post took off from a Beckenham park and landed in France?
fact: In 1902, for Edward VII's coronation, a hot air balloon left this park with mail. It dropped letters in Kent, then crossed the Channel to near Calais.

line: Did you know, Beckenham's Chinese Garage was actually designed to look Japanese?
fact: The roundabout's petrol station was built in 1928 as a Japanese pagoda. Locals called it the Chinese Garage; its real name was Langley Park Garage.

line: Did you know, the River Beck most likely took its name from Beckenham, not the other way round?
fact: Beckenham is thought to mean Beohha's homestead and was recorded in 862. Its stream, the Beck, was most likely named after the village.

line: Did you know, the gate into Beckenham's churchyard is about 600 years older than the church behind it?
fact: The roofed timber gate into St George's churchyard dates from the 1200s. The church behind it was rebuilt in the 1880s, about 600 years later.

line: Did you know, Enid Blyton's mother thought her writing was a waste of time and money?
fact: Enid Blyton grew up in Beckenham. As a schoolgirl she was offered the chance to print her poems, but her mother called it a waste of time and money.

line: Did you know, for 110 years a Beckenham sports ground was where tennis stars warmed up for Wimbledon?
fact: From 1886 to 1996 a grass-court tournament here was a dress rehearsal for Wimbledon. 33 of its winners went on to win Wimbledon the same year.

line: Did you know, the hospital that gave English the word bedlam moved to Monks Orchard in 1930?
fact: Bethlem hospital, nicknamed Bedlam, was founded in the City of London in 1247; its nickname became the word for chaos. In 1930 it moved out here.

line: Did you know, the Crystal Palace fire was spotted by its manager while out with his daughter, Crystal?
fact: The Crystal Palace burned down in 1936. Its manager saw the first glow while out walking the dog with his daughter Crystal, named after the building.

line: Did you know, the Girl Guides began after girls turned up at a Scout meeting in Crystal Palace Park?
fact: At a Boy Scout meeting at the Crystal Palace in 1909, Robert Baden-Powell saw how keen girls were on Scouting. It led to the Girl Guides.

line: Did you know, during the First World War the Crystal Palace was a navy base called HMS Crystal Palace?
fact: In the First World War the glass palace became a navy training base, known as HMS Crystal Palace. Over 125,000 men trained for war there.

line: Did you know, Formula One cars once raced around the paths of Crystal Palace Park?
fact: From 1927 a motor racing track ran along the park's paths, and Formula One cars raced here. It shut in 1974, once racing in a park was judged unsafe.

line: Did you know, an 1864 railway in Crystal Palace Park sucked its carriage through a tunnel with a giant fan?
fact: In 1864 a huge fan sucked a test railway's carriage along an airtight tunnel here, and back again. Rides cost sixpence and took 50 seconds.

place: Crystal Palace Bowl, Crystal Palace Park
line: Did you know, the Who's drummer once served tea and cake from a rowing boat in Crystal Palace Park?
fact: Hosting a 1972 concert at the park's stage, the Who's drummer Keith Moon flew in by helicopter, then rowed the lake dressed as a pirate, serving tea.

line: Did you know, the marble gorilla by Crystal Palace's lake is a portrait of London Zoo's Guy?
fact: The black marble gorilla by the lake is Guy, a London Zoo favourite. He reached the zoo on Guy Fawkes Day 1947, which is how he got his name.

line: Did you know, Anerley is named after a Scotsman's house called Anerly, Scots for solitary?
fact: In 1827 a Scottish merchant built the first house on old Penge Common and called it Anerly, Scots for solitary. The road and the area took its name.

line: Did you know, Anerley once had pleasure gardens with a boating lake and a maze?
fact: From 1841 rail travellers came to Anerley's pleasure gardens for dances, a boating lake and a maze. They shut in 1868, beaten by the Crystal Palace.

line: Did you know, an Indian MP who lived in Anerley swore his oath to Parliament on a Zoroastrian holy book?
fact: Dadabhai Naoroji lived on Anerley Park from 1897. Elected an MP in 1892 by just 5 votes, he swore his oath on a Zoroastrian holy book, not the Bible.

line: Did you know, Penge's name comes from the language that later became Welsh?
fact: Penge's name is Brittonic, the language that became Welsh, and means head of the wood. A charter of 957 mentions the wood called Penge.

line: Did you know, a Penge street was renamed because of its link to an 1877 murder?
fact: In 1877 an heiress, Harriet Staunton, and her baby son were starved to death by her husband and others. Forbes Road, tied to the case, was renamed.

line: Did you know, the almshouses on Penge High Street were built for retired Thames boatmen?
fact: These almshouses were built in 1840 by the Thames watermen's company for its retired boatmen and their widows. They lived here until 1973.
source: Wikipedia: Free Watermen and Lightermen's Almshouses; Penge

line: Did you know, the railway through Penge West was once a canal?
fact: The line through Penge West follows the Croydon Canal of 1809. It lost money and lasted only 27 years before a railway company bought it.

line: Did you know, Kent House station is named after the first house over the old Surrey border into Kent?
fact: Kent House station, opened in 1884, took its name from Kent House farm, the first house on the Kent side of the old county line with Surrey.

line: Did you know, West Wickham's old manor house was built for a man who married an Anne Boleyn?
fact: Wickham Court was built in 1469 for Sir Henry Heydon, whose wife was Anne Boleyn. Not the queen, but her great-aunt of the same name.

line: Did you know, up to 15,000 people sheltered in the Chislehurst Caves in the Second World War?
fact: From 1940 the old chalk mines became an underground town where each person paid a penny to enter. It had lighting, toilets, a chapel and a hospital.

line: Did you know, the one baby born in the Chislehurst Caves shelter was named Cavena?
fact: She was christened in the cave chapel during the Second World War. At 18 she changed her first name to Rose, keeping Cavena as her middle name.

line: Did you know, the Druid altars in Chislehurst Caves come from a theory nobody ever proved?
fact: In 1903 an archaeologist claimed Druids, Romans and Saxons dug the caves, and the three parts were named after them. In fact they were chalk mines.

line: Did you know, Napoleon III courted the daughter of Camden Place decades before he died there?
fact: In the 1830s the exile often visited Emily Rowles, whose father owned the house. She later helped him escape a French jail. He died here in 1873.

line: Did you know, Napoleon III spent his exile in Chislehurst designing a more efficient stove?
fact: Deposed after the war of 1870, the French emperor settled at Camden Place. He filled his time writing and designing a stove that used less energy.

line: Did you know, Camden Town's name comes from a house in Chislehurst?
fact: Camden Town is named after Earl Camden, whose title came from his estate here, Camden Place. The house was named after historian William Camden.

line: Did you know, Chislehurst's old phone code spelled IMP, for a French prince?
fact: Until 1966 Chislehurst and Bickley numbers began 467, which spells IMP, for the Prince Imperial. Napoleon III's son had lived at nearby Camden Place.

line: Did you know, a French prince killed fighting for the British Army was buried in Chislehurst?
fact: Napoleon III's son trained at Woolwich and was killed in the Zulu War in 1879. Queen Victoria was among 10,000 people at his funeral here.
source: Wikipedia: St Mary's Church, Chislehurst; Napoléon, Prince Imperial

line: Did you know, Chislehurst took on London at cricket on its common in 1738?
fact: The July 1738 match swung several times before London won. The two sides met on the common again in 1740, and London won that one too.

line: Did you know, Christopher Marlowe was staying at Scadbury, in Chislehurst, just before he was killed?
fact: In 1593 the playwright was a guest at Scadbury Manor, home of his patron Thomas Walsingham. The man who killed him was Walsingham's business agent.
source: Wikipedia: Scadbury Park; Thomas Walsingham (literary patron)

line: Did you know, Sydney in Australia is named after a man who owned Scadbury in Chislehurst?
fact: In 1742 the Scadbury estate passed to Thomas Townshend, 1st Viscount Sydney. The Australian city of Sydney was named after him.

line: Did you know, the story goes that summer time was dreamed up on a ride in Petts Wood?
fact: The story goes that builder William Willett got the idea seeing blinds still down one summer morning. His memorial is a sundial set to summer time.

line: Did you know, old legal limits barred any other pub within a mile of Petts Wood's Daylight Inn?
fact: Built in 1935 and named after summer time campaigner William Willett, the Daylight was Petts Wood's only pub until a Wetherspoons opened.

line: Did you know, the campaigner for British Summer Time was an ancestor of Coldplay's singer?
fact: William Willett, who pushed for summer time, was buried at St Nicholas' in 1915. His great-great-grandson is Chris Martin of the band Coldplay.

line: Did you know, Petts Wood is named after a family of shipbuilders?
fact: The name first appeared in 1577, as the wood of the Pett family. They were shipbuilders, and leased the wood for its timber.

line: Did you know, Petts Wood station was paid for by the developer building the suburb around it?
fact: The developer gave the Southern Railway £6,000 to build a station for his new suburb. It opened in 1928, and the houses spread out from there.
source: Wikipedia: Petts Wood; Petts Wood railway station

line: Did you know, Petts Wood was popular with Fleet Street journalists in the 1950s?
fact: Its all-night trains suited reporters and sub-editors coming off late shifts. One writer said it gave them a heaven-sent excuse for one more drink.

line: Did you know, Mottingham's almshouses replaced the Hoxton ones that became the Museum of the Home?
fact: The Ironmongers' Company built Sir Robert Geffrye's almshouses here in 1912, to replace its old ones in Hoxton. Those became the Museum of the Home.

line: Did you know, W. G. Grace shook his fist at German Zeppelins over his Mottingham home?
fact: Told that fast bowlers never unsettled him, the old cricketer replied: "I could see those beggars; I can't see these." He died here in 1915.

line: Did you know, in 1585 the ground in Mottingham opened up and swallowed three elm trees?
fact: One August morning a field sank so fast that three great elms vanished into a pit full of water. It was likely a sinkhole; nobody now knows where.

place: St Paulinus Church, St Paul's Cray
line: Did you know, St Paul's Cray is not named after St Paul?
fact: The name is short for St Paulinus Cray, after an early Christian missionary who became Archbishop of York. His church here is 11th century.

line: Did you know, bells for Canterbury Cathedral were cast in St Mary Cray?
fact: In the 1600s St Mary Cray had bell foundries. One founder, Christopher Hodson, made bells for Canterbury Cathedral and for Oxford.

place: St Mary Cray station, St Mary Cray
line: Did you know, one of London's oldest football clubs began with railway builders in St Mary Cray?
fact: Cray Wanderers trace their start to 1860, when migrant workers came to build the railway here. They first played at Star Lane, now a cemetery.

place: St Mary Cray station, St Mary Cray
line: Did you know, rival Teddy Boy gangs fought at St Mary Cray station in 1954?
fact: It began at a dance, where the MC had the band play calming music, no quicksteps. A fight then broke out at the station and 40 youths were held.

line: Did you know, a 13th-century church at Ruxley was used as a farm building for 400 years?
fact: St Botolph's was closed in 1557, when its parish was folded into North Cray. Farmers then kept their tools in it for over 400 years.

line: Did you know, 50 million year old sharks' teeth lie in a pit opposite Elmstead Woods station?
fact: The pit across from the station shows a layer laid down in an estuary 50 million years ago. It holds fossil sharks' teeth, shells and fish scales.

line: Did you know, Frognal House became a major First World War centre for rebuilding soldiers' faces?
fact: In 1917 the mansion became the first home of Queen's Hospital, the war's major centre for facial and plastic surgery. It admitted 5,000 men by 1921.

line: Did you know, the Orpington chicken was bred black so London's soot wouldn't show?
fact: In the 1880s a local breeder crossed three breeds into a new chicken for eggs and meat. He picked black so city soot and grime wouldn't show.

line: Did you know, a Roman farmhouse was found beside Orpington station by workmen making a driveway?
fact: The villa, with underfloor heating, was lived in from about 140 AD for 260 years. Workmen laying a driveway for new council offices found it in 1926.

line: Did you know, the International Romani Union was founded at a meeting in Orpington?
fact: Romani families came to camps round Orpington each year to pick hops and fruit. In 1971 an international Romani meeting here founded the union.

line: Did you know, the Canadian province of Ontario paid for a war hospital in Orpington?
fact: Built in the First World War for about 1,000 patients, it treated over 25,000 wounded soldiers by 1919. Its prefab buildings lasted 80 years.

line: Did you know, a war cross in Orpington was unveiled with the plunger George V used at the Cenotaph?
fact: Canadian Corner holds 182 soldiers who died at the town's war hospital, 88 of them Canadian. Its cross was unveiled in 1921 using the same plunger.

line: Did you know, a 1962 by-election turned Orpington man into the press's word for suburban voters?
fact: In 1962 the Liberal Party won Orpington, a safe Conservative seat, on a huge swing. The press invented Orpington man to explain the suburban revolt.

line: Did you know, Orpington's old parish church lost its steeple to lightning in 1809?
fact: A storm damaged the tower and steeple of All Saints in 1771. The rebuilt steeple was then struck by lightning in 1809, and it was never put back.

line: Did you know, a 1933 newsreel filmed the funeral of the last Queen of the Kent Gypsies in Farnborough?
fact: British Pathé filmed the funeral of Urania Boswell, the last Queen of the Kent Gypsies, as her coffin was carried into St Giles church in 1933.

line: Did you know, the Princess Royal University Hospital began as a Victorian workhouse?
fact: A workhouse opened at Locksbottom in 1845. By the 1920s it had turned into Farnborough Hospital, rebuilt and renamed the Princess Royal in 2003.

line: Did you know, Green Street Green filled with tea rooms for weekend cyclists from London?
fact: From the 1920s to the 1960s, crowds of weekend cyclists rode out from London's suburbs and met here. Several tea rooms opened to serve them.

line: Did you know, the line through Chelsfield is one of the places linked to The Railway Children?
fact: The line here climbs steadily into Chelsfield Tunnel. The story goes that this stretch inspired the writer E. Nesbit's book The Railway Children.

line: Did you know, Pratt's Bottom is named after a valley and a noble family?
fact: In old place names a bottom is a valley or hollow. The Pratts were a noble family who once had their seat here, so the village became Pratt's Bottom.

line: Did you know, Knockholt station first opened as Halstead, the village it's actually nearer?
fact: It opened in 1876 as Halstead for Knockholt. In 1900 a railway boss who lived in Knockholt got it renamed, after mix-ups with Halstead in Essex.

line: Did you know, Knockholt campaigned its way back out of London four years after joining?
fact: Knockholt was put into the new London Borough of Bromley in 1965. After a determined campaign by its villagers, it was handed back to Kent in 1969.

line: Did you know, Darwin's family turned their backs during one creed at Downe church?
fact: Charles Darwin's wife Emma was a Unitarian. So whenever the church's Trinity creed was read at St Mary's, the family turned to face away.

line: Did you know, a slope near Downe gave Darwin the evidence for his book on orchids?
fact: Darwin called this chalk bank Orchis Bank for its wild orchids. Watching them and their insect pollinators gave him the evidence for his 1862 book.

line: Did you know, the man who gave Britain its bank holidays grew up at High Elms?
fact: John Lubbock, a banker and MP raised on the High Elms estate, brought in the 1871 law that created bank holidays. Some called them St Lubbock's Days.

line: Did you know, a boy at High Elms was let down when 1842's big news was Darwin, not a pony?
fact: Young John Lubbock hoped his father's big news was a new pony. It was only Charles Darwin moving to Downe. The boy became a close friend of Darwin's.

line: Did you know, Biggin Hill airfield started out defending London from Zeppelins?
fact: Long before the Battle of Britain, the Royal Flying Corps came here in 1917 for one huge open field. Its job was to fight off Zeppelins and bombers.

line: Did you know, Biggin Hill's St Mark's church was built from a taken-apart church in Peckham?
fact: Known as the moving church, it went up in the 1950s from the taken-apart materials of All Saints, North Peckham. Volunteers did much of the work.

line: Did you know, local historians say Biggin Hill's Old Jail pub held French prisoners of war?
fact: Two local history groups say the 1700s building was used to hold French prisoners overnight in Napoleon's time, on their way to Maidstone.

line: Did you know, a post on Leaves Green marked where the City of London could tax coal?
fact: Coal tax post number 186, on the village green, marked the edge of the area where the City of London Corporation was allowed to charge a duty on coal.

line: Did you know, cyclists raced up Westerham Hill on penny-farthings in 1887?
fact: A Catford cycling club held one of the earliest cycle hill climbs here in 1887, on a steep road with no hard surface. Half of the 24 riders made it.
